texts: A lantern at the Sunken Cove dies before dawn.
What emerges from the water of the Sunken Cove?

good. the lantern, the Sunken Cove as a named place with its kind, the lantern's position there, the dying, and the "before dawn" deadline are all carried, and no tense is invented for the bare present.

good. it asks for whatever emerges, with the cove's water as what it emerges from, and it reuses the Sunken Cove from the previous sentence instead of re-identifying it. One caution rather than a rewrite: it looks for the emerging thing as the doer of the emergence, so an answering sentence that presents it as carried or pushed up rather than moving under its own power would file it in a different slot and the question would miss it.
A lantern burns wintergloss alongside mire-essence.

mixed: the lantern burning wintergloss is recorded correctly, but "alongside mire-essence" only lands as a loose "alongside" modifier on the burning, so nothing says the mire-essence is burned too and the second substance drops out of the fuel claim. Rewrite as "A lantern burns wintergloss and mire-essence." — coordinated objects each get their own burning, so both substances are recorded as burned.

good. it asks what wintergloss does, and it uses the wintergloss symbol from the previous sentence directly instead of re-identifying it. One caution rather than a rewrite: the question asks for wintergloss as the doer, while your own premise stores it only as the substance being burned, so nothing will answer unless the knowledge base elsewhere has wintergloss acting.
The feather store at the Watch is large.
What does each Keeper do in winter?
good. the feather store, its position at the Watch, and its largeness are all carried, and "the Watch" stays a plain definite rather than an invented proper name.

good. it asks for the activity with a Keeper as the doer and winter as the time. Two cautions rather than a rewrite: "each" has no carrier in a question and is dropped, so it effectively asks what a Keeper does; and if the Keepers' winter work is stated generically it is stored as a rule about Keepers in general, so the question returns something only once some individual Keeper is in the knowledge base.
A wraith drains the lanterns of the West Row.
The drained lanterns attract a handful of nightmoths.
What happens to the thread harvest?
good. the wraith, the draining, the lanterns as one definite set being drained, and the named West Row with its kind are all carried.

bad: two losses. "drained" is dropped entirely, so nothing records that the lanterns are in a drained state, and the per-lantern rule the parse adds hands every single lantern the same handful of nightmoths — claiming each lantern separately attracts the whole handful, which you say only of the lanterns as a set. Rewrite as "The lanterns are drained, and together they attract a handful of nightmoths." — the separate clause gives "drained" somewhere to land, and "together" keeps the attracting collective so the count stays with the group.

bad: "what happens to X" has no question form the translator can build — the harvest is hung off a bare "to" modifier that no statement would ever fill (and which can collide with the purpose "to" of another sentence), so the question asks for an event aimed at the harvest rather than one that befalls it, and it binds nothing. Name the event and make the harvest its object: "What ruins the thread harvest?" — substitute the verb you actually mean (eat, spoil, ruin), so the harvest sits in the object slot an answering sentence would really use.
A lantern on the Middle Row is untended through the night.

mixed: the untended state, the lantern and the Middle Row are all recorded correctly, but "through the night" leaves only a day-part time stamp — the claim that the lantern stays untended for the whole span is dropped, because a definite period with no stated count has no duration carrier. Rewrite it as a counted duration: "A lantern on the Middle Row is untended for one night."

mixed: the query correctly reuses the lantern's symbol and leaves the verb open, but an open "happens to" question forces a guess at the undergoer's role and it guesses Patient, while the premise stores the lantern only as the untended state's experiencer, so the question matches nothing; the only licensed open-verb template is the agent-side "What does X do?". Name the consequence you are probing for and ask it plainly, e.g. "Does the lantern go out?"
The lanterns of three Cliff Path stations burn extra mire-essence.
What happens to the lanterns of those stations?

bad: the per-lantern rule hands every lantern one and the same portion of mire-essence (it reuses a single essence symbol as each lantern's object), which the sentence does not say, and "extra" on a mass noun has no licensed quantity carrier, so it lands on an invented marker. Rewrite so each lantern gets its own countable portion and "extra" can ride as an ordinary adjective: "Each lantern of the three Cliff Path stations burns an extra ration of mire-essence."

mixed: the query correctly reuses the lanterns' group symbol, but with the verb left open the undergoer's role has to be guessed, and it guesses Patient while the premise stores these lanterns as the burning event's agent, so nothing binds. Either name the consequence — "Do the lanterns of those stations burn out?" — or, to keep the verb open, use the one licensed open template, "What do the lanterns of those stations do?", which binds the stored burning event.
The Stilllight Lantern burns wintergloss alongside mire-essence for one week.

mixed: the lantern's name, the one-week duration and the burnt wintergloss are all right, but "alongside mire-essence" survives only as a bare surface oblique on the burning event — nothing records that the mire-essence is burned too, since the co-participant role is animate-only. Rewrite it as plain coordination so both substances are recorded as burnt: "The Stilllight Lantern burns wintergloss and mire-essence for one week."

good. it is the licensed "What does X do?" template with the context's wintergloss constant in the agent slot, which is exactly what the question asks; note only that the premise records wintergloss solely as the substance burned, so as worded the question has no agent-side fact to find.
A Keeper dims a lantern on the Cliff Path.
The dim lantern attracts a handful of nightmoths.
What happens to the thread harvest?
good. the dimming event carries its Keeper agent and its lantern patient, and "on the Cliff Path" correctly stays a property of the lantern rather than of the dimming.
good. it reuses the lantern from the first sentence, adds only the stated "dim" property, and records "a handful" as a vague-count phrase on the nightmoth group instead of inventing a number.

bad: the harvest is attached with a surface "to" oblique, so the query asks which events are directed at the harvest rather than which eventuality befalls it — a slot no ordinary statement fills — and that same shape is the purpose connective, which the engine's purpose bridge can misread as a goal; nothing about the harvest can bind, and the two premises mention no thread harvest at all. Name the focus event and put the harvest in the role a plain statement would store it in, e.g. "Do the nightmoths damage the thread harvest?"
